paragraphs: The paper studies learning through repeated correction: an algorithm proposes a model, and a user either accepts it or identifies a particular mistake. The same interaction can describe learning a classifier, a ranking, or a clustering. The challenge is to reach the true model with few rounds even when some corrections are deliberately misleading.

The authors represent possible models as nodes in a graph, with weighted edges representing feedback. Their central sufficient condition is geometric: every correct correction must point along a shortest path from the proposed model to the target. This turns different kinds of learning problems into a shared problem of navigating a graph.

When feedback is correct with probability greater than one half, an algorithm resembling multiplicative weights can efficiently learn the target under this graph condition. Incorrect feedback may otherwise be arbitrary. The framework recovers existing classification and clustering results and yields new ranking algorithms, showing how one structural condition can support several forms of robust interaction.
neurips-2017-a-general-framework-for-rob.tldr: A graph-based framework efficiently learns from noisy corrections when correct feedback follows shortest paths toward the target model.

paragraphs: Reconstructing neurons from three-dimensional electron microscope images requires deciding which image regions belong to the same object. The paper separates checking and repairing these decisions into two learning tasks. Both receive the original image together with a binary mask marking a candidate object, so the networks can examine image evidence alongside an existing segmentation.

The detection task produces a spatial map of split and merge errors. The correction task instead aims to output the true object. The authors call correction object mask pruning because they assume the candidate mask already contains the entire true object. Under that assumption, correction involves removing unwanted portions from a sufficiently inclusive candidate.

The authors train multiscale three-dimensional convolutional networks for both tasks and report high accuracy for detection. Correction improves when the detector supplies advice in the form of a union of erroneous objects. This finding supports connecting detection to correction: identifying problematic pieces can help construct the input from which the correction network recovers the intended object.
neurips-2017-an-error-detection-and-corr.tldr: Separate 3D networks detect segmentation errors and improve object correction by supplying detector-generated candidate masks.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial learning trains a generator against a discriminator to approximate a data distribution. This paper asks what that competition actually guarantees. It examines how limiting the discriminator's available functions changes approximation quality, and when improving the training objective means that the generated distribution is approaching the target in a mathematical sense.

The authors introduce adversarial divergences, a shared mathematical framework encompassing several proposed adversarial objectives. Within this framework, they show that restricting the discriminator has a moment-matching effect when additional conditions hold. In plain language, the restriction makes agreement on certain statistical summaries central to the comparison between generated and target data.

A second result connects objective convergence to distributional convergence: for strict adversarial divergences, convergence of the objective implies weak convergence of distributions. The significance is conditional and precise. Appropriate objectives can make progress in their numerical value meaningful as distributional progress, while the discriminator analysis explains how its expressive restrictions shape what the learning problem measures.
neurips-2017-approximation-and-convergen.tldr: The paper characterizes how restricted discriminators shape GAN approximation and when objective convergence implies weak distributional convergence.

paragraphs: An image caption can be broadly appropriate while saying little about what makes its particular image distinctive. This paper treats that distinction as an important part of caption quality. Its aim is to encourage descriptions that capture unique aspects of an image while preserving the overall quality of the generated language.

The proposed method, Contrastive Learning, adds two constraints formulated relative to a reference model. These constraints are intended to encourage distinctiveness while maintaining caption quality. The contribution therefore concerns the learning method: it gives captioning models an additional way to favor informative descriptions, with the reference model providing a basis for the formulation.

Experiments on two challenging datasets show substantial improvements over the baseline model. The authors also study different model structures and find that the method can be used across them. These results support distinctiveness as a useful training goal and suggest that the approach is applicable to multiple captioning architectures, rather than depending on one particular network design.
neurips-2017-contrastive-learning-for-im.tldr: Contrastive Learning improves image captioning by encouraging distinctive descriptions while maintaining overall caption quality.

paragraphs: Similar recurrent circuit patterns appear across different areas of the cortex, raising the possibility that they implement shared computational principles. This paper explores that possibility through a recurrent neural network inspired by long short-term memory networks. The aim is to connect a useful machine learning computation with the organization of cortical circuits.

The proposed subLSTM gates information using subtractive inhibitory cells. The authors describe a natural mapping between these units and known cortical microcircuits containing excitatory and inhibitory cells. That mapping makes the network a concrete computational proposal for how familiar circuit components could support gated processing of information across a sequence.

In sequential image classification and language modelling experiments, subLSTM units achieve performance similar to LSTM units. This provides evidence that the proposed form of inhibition can support demanding contextual tasks. The findings suggest a possible computational role for cortical circuitry and a connection to trainable recurrent networks; they do not establish that biological circuits use the proposed mechanism exactly.
neurips-2017-cortical-microcircuits-as-g.tldr: SubLSTM connects subtractive inhibitory gating to cortical microcircuits and achieves performance similar to LSTMs on sequential tasks.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems call for a guaranteed directional relationship between selected inputs and the output. A monotonic model preserves that relationship as those inputs change. This paper develops deep networks that are monotonic with respect to inputs specified by the user, allowing those requirements to be built into a jointly trained model.

The architecture alternates linear embedding layers, ensembles of lattices, and calibrators, which are piecewise linear functions. Appropriate constraints on these components enforce monotonicity throughout the resulting network. The authors implement the layers and constraint projections as new TensorFlow computational graph nodes, and train using Adam with batched stochastic gradients.

Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets show that six-layer monotonic deep lattice networks achieve state-of-the-art classification and regression performance. The contribution combines predictive performance with guarantees about how selected inputs affect predictions. Because the user chooses the constrained inputs, the approach addresses partial monotonicity rather than requiring the same directional structure for every input.
neurips-2017-deep-lattice-networks-and-p.tldr: Deep lattice networks combine competitive prediction with guaranteed monotonic behavior for user-selected inputs.

paragraphs: ELF is a platform for reinforcement learning research built around fast, configurable game environments. The authors implement a real-time strategy engine with Mini-RTS, Capture the Flag, and Tower Defense. Mini-RTS preserves key dynamics of a larger strategy game while running at 165,000 frames per second on a laptop, enabling substantial simulated experience.

The platform supports different arrangements for communication between environments and agents, different learning methods, and changes to game parameters. It can also host existing C/C++ game environments. With six CPUs and one GPU, the reported system trains a bot end to end against built-in opponents in one day.

The authors investigate training choices and report that Leaky ReLU, Batch Normalization, long-horizon training, and a progressive curriculum together produce a Mini-RTS agent that beats the rule-based opponent more than 70% of the time. They also report strong performance in the other games and interesting strategies in replays. These findings demonstrate the platform's usefulness for testing how training choices affect complete game behavior.
neurips-2017-elf-an-extensive-lightweigh.tldr: ELF provides fast, configurable strategy games that support end-to-end reinforcement learning and systematic experiments with training choices.

paragraphs: Fader Networks aim to make image attributes directly adjustable after a model has been trained. The proposed encoder-decoder learns to reconstruct images while separating salient image information from attribute values in its latent representation. This organization allows the decoder to create different versions of the same input as the supplied attributes change.

The attribute values can vary continuously, so editing can control how strongly an attribute appears rather than merely switching it on or off. The authors suggest interfaces resembling mixing-console sliders, with possible uses such as changing a portrait's expression or an object's color. These are applications enabled by the model's continuous controls.

The paper reports a simpler training scheme than approaches that largely rely on adversarial training in pixel space while changing attributes during training. It also states that the method scales well to multiple attributes. The presented evidence shows substantial changes in perceived attributes while maintaining natural-looking images, supporting the idea that separating attribute controls in latent space can make image manipulation practical.
neurips-2017-fader-networks-manipulating.tldr: Fader Networks separate image content and attributes in latent space to enable continuous, natural-looking image edits.

paragraphs: Some matrix problems receive a large positive-semidefinite matrix through a stream of linear updates. Storing the full matrix may be impractical, leaving only a compact sketch available for later computation. This paper addresses how to recover a fixed-rank positive-semidefinite approximation from that sketch, a problem relevant to streaming PCA and semidefinite programming.

The proposed algorithm combines the Nyström approximation with a new mechanism for truncating rank. The rank constraint controls the size of the resulting approximation, while preserving positive semidefiniteness keeps its structure compatible with the original matrix problem. The contribution is a way to perform this reconstruction using the retained sketch.

The theoretical analysis shows that the method can achieve any prescribed relative error in the Schatten 1-norm and benefits from spectral decay in the input matrix. Experiments report superiority over alternative fixed-rank approximation techniques across a broad collection of examples. Together, these results support both a mathematical accuracy guarantee and practical effectiveness when storage constraints make full-matrix methods unsuitable.
neurips-2017-fixed-rank-approximation-of.tldr: A new Nyström-based method reconstructs fixed-rank positive-semidefinite approximations from sketches with relative-error guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering function values from noisy observations on a regular multidimensional grid with equal side lengths. The function is assumed to be smooth, but different regions may have different amounts of smoothness. A useful mathematical description must therefore accommodate local variation without imposing the same behavior everywhere on the grid.

Classical Hölder smoothness does not capture this heterogeneity well. Total variation allows heterogeneous behavior, but assigns zero variation only to constant functions. The authors introduce two higher-order total variation classes using different ways of collecting discrete derivatives across grid nodes. These classes broaden how smoothness can be expressed while retaining the motivation for allowing regional differences.

The analysis relates both new classes to Hölder classes and establishes minimax lower bounds, which describe unavoidable estimation error over each class. The authors also study two corresponding trend filtering methods. In two dimensions, each method attains the optimal error rate for its associated class, connecting the proposed smoothness descriptions to estimators with matching statistical guarantees.
neurips-2017-higher-order-total-variatio.tldr: Two higher-order total variation classes describe heterogeneous grid smoothness and yield rate-optimal trend filtering methods in two dimensions.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because an agent receives little direct feedback about progress. Hindsight Experience Replay is proposed as a way to learn efficiently when rewards simply indicate success or failure. Its practical aim is to make these simple reward definitions usable without designing a more complicated reward signal.

The technique can be combined with any off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm and can be interpreted as an implicit curriculum. The authors evaluate it using a robotic arm on pushing, sliding, and pick-and-place tasks. In all three cases, the reward is binary and reports only whether the requested task has been completed.

Ablation studies identify Hindsight Experience Replay as a crucial component that makes training possible in these challenging environments. The authors also deploy policies learned in physics simulation on a physical robot and report successful task completion. These results connect learning from minimal feedback to physical execution, showing that the approach's benefits in the reported tasks extend beyond simulated training.
neurips-2017-hindsight-experience-replay.tldr: Hindsight Experience Replay enables efficient learning from sparse binary rewards and supports successful transfer from simulated manipulation to a physical robot.

paragraphs: Local aggregative games model situations where a player's payoff depends on its own action and the combined behavior of neighboring players. A connected directed graph describes who influences whom. The paper studies both the strategic behavior supported by this model and the problem of learning the graph and payoff functions.

The authors establish the existence of pure-strategy approximate Nash equilibria when payoff functions are convex or submodular. Such an equilibrium allows only a limited benefit from an individual changing its action. They also prove an information-theoretic lower bound for approximating the graph structure in a value-oracle setting with specified nonnegative, monotone submodular edge-set costs.

The paper introduces gamma-aggregative games as a generalization with approximate equilibria stable under small changes to a specified graph property. It also presents estimation algorithms that meaningfully recover structure and payoffs from real voting data. The contribution thus links conditional equilibrium guarantees, limits on learning the interaction structure, and evidence that the model can capture patterns in observed collective decisions.
neurips-2017-local-aggregative-games-ad5.tldr: The paper studies equilibrium, structural learning limits, and estimation in games driven by neighboring players' aggregate behavior.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering often approximates a user-item rating matrix with low-rank models, representing users and items through a limited number of features. Standard approaches typically use the same rank throughout. The authors' studies indicate that different submatrices can have different ranks, suggesting that a single shared rank may miss important internal structure.

The proposed mixture-rank matrix approximation represents ratings using a mixture of low-rank models with different ranks. This gives the overall model a way to express multiple levels of structural complexity within one rating matrix. To fit it, the authors develop a learning algorithm based on iterated condition modes for the resulting nonconvex optimization problem.

Experiments on MovieLens and Netflix show that the proposed method can exceed the recommendation accuracy of six state-of-the-art low-rank collaborative filtering methods. The finding supports adapting representation complexity to variation within the ratings. It provides empirical evidence for the mixture approach on these datasets, rather than establishing that every rating matrix requires models of multiple ranks.
neurips-2017-mixture-rank-matrix-approxi.tldr: Mixing matrix models of different ranks improves recommendation accuracy by accommodating varying structure within user-item ratings.

paragraphs: Net-Trim reduces the number of connections in an already trained ReLU network. It processes each layer through a convex optimization problem that seeks sparse weights while keeping the layer's input-output behavior consistent with the original model. This makes pruning an explicitly constrained approximation problem rather than simply discarding connections without checking their effect.

The paper presents parallel and cascade versions. The parallel version supports distributed computation, while the cascade version can produce slightly simpler models with the same generalization performance. Both substantially reduce connections, and the reported regularization effect slightly lowers generalization error. The authors also mathematically analyze consistency between the original and modified networks.

A separate sample-complexity result gives sufficient conditions for recovering a sparse transformation. For one layer with independent Gaussian input vectors of length N and at most s nonzero weights per node, the weights can be learned from order s log N samples. This guarantee applies to that stated input and sparsity setting, providing a concrete theoretical basis for sparse recovery within the broader pruning approach.
neurips-2017-net-trim-convex-pruning-of-.tldr: Net-Trim uses convex layerwise optimization to sparsify trained ReLU networks while controlling consistency with their original behavior.

paragraphs: Neural program induction learns an input-output mapping from examples, but learning each new task separately can demand substantial data and computation. This paper investigates transferring knowledge from related tasks. The aim is to make program induction more effective when a new task provides only a small collection of input-output examples.

The authors propose two approaches. Portfolio adaptation pretrains several induction models on related tasks, selects the best model, and adapts it to the new task. Meta program induction instead learns to handle new tasks from a few examples without additional training. They evaluate both using a newly constructed benchmark of Karel programs.

Both approaches strongly outperform the evaluated induction baseline without transfer, but their relative strengths depend on data availability. Meta induction performs best among the compared approaches with fewer than ten examples. Portfolio adaptation becomes strongest with a thousand or more examples. For intermediate amounts of data, adapting a meta-induction model performs best, showing that the most effective transfer strategy changes with the available evidence.
neurips-2017-neural-program-meta-inducti.tldr: Transferring knowledge across program-induction tasks improves learning, with different transfer strategies winning at different data sizes.

paragraphs: Finding heavy hitters means identifying frequently occurring values among participants' data. This paper develops two algorithms, TreeHist and Bitstogram, for doing so under local differential privacy. Their main contribution is to combine optimal or nearly optimal worst-case error with substantially lower computation requirements for both the collecting server and individual users.

Ignoring logarithmic factors, server computation grows linearly with the number of participants, while each user's computation is constant. The prior result discussed in the abstract required server time growing as the number of users to the power 2.5 and user time growing to the power 1.5. This changes how the workload scales as participation increases.

The improvement is particularly relevant when local privacy systems involve millions of participants, where expensive processing on every user's side can obstruct deployment. The authors implement TreeHist to check their theoretical analysis and compare it with Google's RAPPOR implementation. The abstract reports this practical evaluation alongside the complexity guarantees without stating a specific numerical outcome for that comparison.
neurips-2017-practical-locally-private-h.tldr: TreeHist and Bitstogram make locally private heavy-hitter detection computationally practical while retaining optimal or near-optimal worst-case error.

paragraphs: Predicting a label from an input often relies on estimating its conditional probability. Conventional models can make strong assumptions about the distribution producing the data, making their answers sensitive to whether those assumptions hold. This paper develops a way to reason about conditional probabilities while imposing much less structure on that distribution.

The framework assumes knowledge only of second-order marginals, which can be estimated from data. It uses this information to derive guaranteed bounds on conditional probabilities, rather than committing to a fully specified underlying distribution. The bounds express what the available marginal information supports while leaving other aspects of the distribution unspecified.

The authors show that these bounds can be computed efficiently in several settings, including structured prediction. They also apply the framework to semi-supervised deep learning and report results competitive with variational autoencoders. The contribution connects robustness to a concrete form of available information: the guarantees rely on the stated marginal knowledge, while the experiments demonstrate that this approach can also support useful learning performance.
neurips-2017-robust-conditional-probabil.tldr: The framework derives guaranteed conditional-probability bounds from second-order marginals without specifying a full underlying distribution.

paragraphs: This paper extends efficient, noise-tolerant learning theory to s-concave distributions, a broader family than log-concave distributions. The family includes important additional examples such as Pareto and t distributions. Studying it enlarges the range of distributional settings for which learning methods can receive sample-efficiency and computational guarantees.

The extension introduces geometric difficulties. Many distributions in the family have heavy tails, and the family is not closed under marginalization. The authors develop convex geometry tools to handle these properties. They bound quantities describing how often two halfspaces disagree, how much disagreement occurs outside a band, and the disagreement coefficient.

These bounds support generalizations of earlier results for margin-based active learning, disagreement-based active learning, and passive learning of intersections of halfspaces. The contribution is therefore both geometric and algorithmic: properties of a broader distribution family become tools for proving learning guarantees. The authors also suggest that their geometric analysis may be useful in optimization, presenting this as a possible further application.
neurips-2017-sample-and-computationally-.tldr: New geometric tools extend efficient learning guarantees to the broader, potentially heavy-tailed family of s-concave distributions.

paragraphs: A prediction model often supplies information to a larger decision process, yet its training criterion may differ from the criterion used to judge the final decision. This paper addresses that mismatch. It proposes training probabilistic models with the ultimate task objective directly in view, within the setting of stochastic optimization.

The approach treats model learning and downstream use as an end-to-end problem. Because the model represents uncertainty for a stochastic program, its value depends on the decisions that program makes using it. Aligning learning with the task objective connects the model's training target to the outcome the full process is intended to achieve.

The authors evaluate the method on an inventory stock problem, real-world electrical grid scheduling, and real-world energy storage arbitrage. In these applications, it can outperform both traditional modeling and purely black-box policy optimization. The findings support learning probabilistic models according to their decision consequences, with the reported advantage demonstrated across three different optimization tasks.
neurips-2017-task-based-end-to-end-model.tldr: Training probabilistic models directly for downstream optimization objectives can improve decisions in inventory and energy applications.

paragraphs: GAN training involves two interacting players, so understanding its numerical behavior requires examining their joint updates. This paper models training as a smooth two-player game and studies the gradient vector field associated with the objective. The focus is on why commonly used training algorithms can have difficulty converging.

The analysis identifies two potentially troublesome features in the eigenvalues of the gradient field's Jacobian: zero real parts and large imaginary parts. These quantities describe aspects of the local update dynamics. The findings suggest that both features contribute to convergence problems, providing specific mathematical targets for changing the training algorithm.

Using this diagnosis, the authors design an algorithm with better convergence properties that addresses some of the identified limitations. Experiments show advantages on common GAN architectures and convergence on architectures described as especially difficult to train. The contribution joins an analysis of training dynamics with an algorithm motivated by that analysis, while the stated improvement concerns some numerical obstacles rather than a universal solution to GAN training.
neurips-2017-the-numerics-of-gans-c6b695.tldr: Analyzing GAN training as a two-player dynamical system reveals numerical obstacles and motivates an algorithm with improved convergence.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how an online independent component analysis algorithm evolves in high dimensions. It tracks the joint empirical distribution of coordinates in the target feature vector and the algorithm's estimates. As dimension grows without bound, with appropriately rescaled time, this distribution converges weakly to a deterministic process.

That limiting process is characterized by the unique solution of a nonlinear partial differential equation with two spatial variables and one time variable. The equation can be solved numerically with practical efficiency. Because many performance measures are functions of the joint empirical distribution, its solution provides detailed predictions about the algorithm's behavior.

Simulations show that the asymptotic description remains accurate at moderate dimensions. The analysis also reveals that coupled coordinate dynamics become decoupled in the limit, with each coordinate behaving like stochastic gradient descent on an effective one-dimensional minimization problem. This supplies an interpretable picture of the algorithm, while using that picture to design better computational-statistical tradeoffs is identified as future research.
neurips-2017-the-scaling-limit-of-high-d.tldr: A deterministic PDE describes high-dimensional online ICA dynamics and gives accurate performance predictions even at moderate dimensions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for learning variational autoencoders using Stein variational gradient descent. Its central advantage concerns the encoder distribution: the method does not require a parametric assumption about its form. This removes a particular modeling restriction from the encoder while retaining the variational autoencoder setting for learning.

The authors also combine the proposed encoder with importance sampling and report that this further improves performance. These are two linked parts of the contribution: the Stein-based approach changes how the encoder distribution is handled, and the importance-sampling integration improves the resulting method. The stated flexibility concerns the encoder's distributional form.

Evaluation covers multiple unsupervised and semi-supervised problems, with strong reported performance across them. The experiments include semi-supervised analysis of ImageNet, providing evidence that the method can operate on a large dataset. Together, the results connect a less restrictive encoder formulation to practical learning performance and scalability across the evaluated problems.
neurips-2017-vae-learning-via-stein-vari.tldr: Stein variational gradient descent enables VAE learning without a prescribed parametric encoder distribution, with further gains from importance sampling.

paragraphs: Variational Walkback learns a stochastic transition operator that generates samples through repeated application. Traditional energy-based approaches learn this behavior indirectly through a Markov chain constrained by detailed balance. The paper instead directly trains the transition rule, allowing more general dynamics, including stationary distributions that do not satisfy detailed balance.

The training objective is derived using variational methods. Starting from observed data points, it encourages multi-step trajectories to return toward their original points quickly. This formulation permits asymmetric neural networks and non-energy-based dynamical systems. The freedom from detailed balance broadens the kinds of transitions the learned model can represent.

Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN, and CelebA produce better samples than earlier attempts to learn transition operators. Although training uses trajectories with finite, variable lengths, the learned operator continues producing good samples well beyond those lengths. This empirical result supports the authors' claim that its non-equilibrium stationary behavior matches the data distribution, connecting short training trajectories with sustained sample generation.
neurips-2017-variational-walkback-learni.tldr: Variational Walkback directly learns stochastic transitions that generate good samples without requiring detailed balance.

paragraphs: Mode collapse occurs when a generative model captures only a few modes of the distribution it is supposed to learn. VEEGAN addresses this problem by adding a reconstructor network to a GAN. The reconstructor maps data back to noise, reversing the generator's direction and making this reverse mapping part of training.

The training objective can be understood as an autoencoder loss over noise and retains the original asymptotic consistency guarantee of GANs. It requires a loss over the representations, assumed to follow a standard normal distribution, rather than a reconstruction loss over data points. This moves the reconstruction comparison into the specified representation space.

Across synthetic and real-world image datasets, the authors find that VEEGAN resists mode collapse substantially better than other recent GAN variants and generates more realistic samples. The results support the reverse-mapping objective as a useful way to improve coverage and sample quality. The empirical claim is reduced collapse, while the theoretical claim concerns asymptotic consistency of the training objective.
neurips-2017-veegan-reducing-mode-collap.tldr: VEEGAN adds a data-to-noise reconstructor that reduces mode collapse while preserving GANs' asymptotic consistency guarantee.

paragraphs: Zap Q-learning modifies Q-learning using a matrix gain, with the aim of improving both long-run statistical behavior and the speed of learning. The algorithm is designed to have optimal asymptotic variance. This criterion concerns variability in its asymptotic behavior, giving the update design an explicit statistical target.

The matrix gain is adjusted through an update equation operating on two time scales. An ordinary differential equation analysis suggests that the algorithm's transient behavior closely resembles a deterministic Newton-Raphson implementation. This connects the proposed learning dynamics to an established root-finding approach and provides a reason to expect efficient progress before reaching the asymptotic regime.

The analysis also suggests stable, efficient computation in non-ideal parameterized settings, and numerical experiments show rapid convergence even in those cases. The paper thus combines an optimal asymptotic-variance design with analytical indications and empirical evidence about convergence speed. The claims about transient behavior and stability remain suggestions from the analysis, supported by the reported experiments.
neurips-2017-zap-q-learning-2987405621.tldr: Zap Q-learning uses a two-time-scale matrix gain designed for optimal asymptotic variance and demonstrates fast numerical convergence.
